queries.hook: I'm anxious about how things will turn out. Inside, my mind won't settle, and I don't know how to carry it.
queries.diagnose: The mind suffers when it clings to results it cannot control; gripping the outcome turns honest effort into anxiety.
queries.steady: Your part is the effort, not the outcome; work done well is already complete, whatever result comes.
queries.act: Do your work fully and well, then let the result go; your part is the effort, not the fruit.

hook.speaker: Bhasa
hook.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
hook.sanskrit: उह्यमानमनन्तेषु चेतः कार्यमहोर्मिषु । क्षणमेति न विश्रान्तिं चिन्ताताण्डविताशयम् ॥ इदं कृतं करोमीदं करिष्यामीदमित्यलम् । कलनाजालवलिता मूर्च्छिता मतिपक्षिणी ॥
hook.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
hook.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.
hook.why: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.

prasang.title: Two old friends meet again and admit they never found peace
prasang.summary: Bhasa and Vilasa grow up inseparable in a forest hermitage. After their fathers die they drift apart and spend long lonely years in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, one asks if the other is well; he answers honestly that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries.
prasang.story_hook: They had been inseparable as boys, and when they met again they were old men with nothing to show.
prasang.lesson: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.

hook.for_you: Your mind won't settle while you are studying, and a verse was chosen with that weight in mind.

alternates.speaker: Yudhishthira
alternates.setting: At a poisoned lake, a Yaksha quizzes Yudhishthira; his brothers' lives hang on the answers.
alternates.sanskrit: किंस्विद्गुरुतरं भूमेः किंस्विदुच्चतरं च स्वात् / किंस्विच्छीघ्रतरं वायोः किंस्विद्बहुतरं तृणात् माता गुरुतरा भूमेः खात्पितोच्चतरस्तथा / मनः शीघ्रतरं वाताच्चिन्ता बहुतरी तृणात्
alternates.line: The mind is faster than the wind, and worries outnumber the blades of grass.
alternates.translation: Yaksha: 'What is heavier than the earth? What is higher than the sky? What is faster than the wind? What is more numerous than blades of grass?' Yudhishthira: 'A mother is heavier than the earth; a father is higher than the sky; the mind is faster than the wind; worries are more numerous than blades of grass.'
alternates.why: Answer life's questions with a steady mind, and let kindness outweigh advantage.

prasang.title: Yaksha Prashna: the questions at the lake
prasang.summary: One by one, four Pandavas drink from a lake against a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's riddles instead, and when offered one brother's life, chooses his stepmother's son Nakula, out of fairness.
prasang.story_hook: Four brothers lay dead by a clear lake, and the voice that killed them was asking Yudhishthira riddles.
prasang.lesson: Answer life's questions with a steady mind, and let kindness outweigh advantage.

alternates.speaker: Rama
alternates.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
alternates.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
alternates.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.
alternates.why: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
alternates.misuse: Holding tears in is not strength. Rama's healing began when he finally said it aloud.

prasang.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. verse.speaker: Bhushunda
verse.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
verse.sanskrit: किमद्य मम संपन्नं प्रातर्वा भविता पुनः । इति चिन्ताज्वरो नास्ति तेन जीवाम्यनामयः ॥
verse.line: 'What happened today? What comes tomorrow?' I don't run that fever. That's why I live well.
verse.translation: 'What has happened to me today? What will come tomorrow?' I have no such fever of worry; so I live long, free of illness.
verse.why: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.

prasang.title: Bhushunda, the crow who outlived the ages
prasang.summary: Vasishtha travels to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has watched world-ages come and go. Asked how he has lived so long, untroubled, Bhushunda lists his habits: he doesn't brood on the past or future, doesn't fret about what he'll get next, doesn't grow arrogant from knowing, and shares in others' joys and sorrows.
prasang.story_hook: High on a mountain lived a crow who had watched whole ages of the world rise and fall.
prasang.lesson: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: Letter from Belur, March 1898, to brother monks running a new centre.
verse.line: The Lord is watching over us; there is no fear; do not lose your nerves, keep your health and take things easy.
verse.translation: Do look after Alasinga. I have an idea that he is breaking himself with work. Tell him, the best work is only done by alternate repose and work. Give him all my love. We had two public lectures in Calcutta, one from Miss Noble and the other from our Sharat. Both of them did very well indeed; there was great enthusiasm, which shows that the Calcutta public has not forgotten us. Some of the members of the Math had a touch of influenza. They are all right now. The thing is working nicely. Shri (Holy) Mother is here, and the European and American ladies went the other day to see her, and what do you think, Mother ate with them even there! Is not that grand? The Lord is watching over us; there is no fear; do not lose your nerves, keep your health and take things easy. It is always good to give a few strong strokes and rest on your oars. Rakhal is living with the new land and buildings. I was not satisfied with the Mahotsava this year. What it should be is a grand mixture of all the different phases here. We shall try it next year — I shall send instructions. With love to all of you there and blessings.

verse.line: In a crisis, you may be shaken inside. Don't let fear make your decisions for you.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.

why: Courage and steadiness are the wheels of the chariot that wins; do not let fear decide.
